graphit: Where the citing literature engages GraphIt, it is mainly as a performance bar. Hardware and accelerator papers measure against its generated code — GraphLily on FPGAs, Capstan for sparsity, work on SpMV-based graph processing — and architecture studies such as Pipette and Dalorex run its programs as workloads, while a GAP-suite evaluation of graph frameworks includes it among those compared. A smaller thread engages the compiler itself, as GraphAttack and Grafs do, and Allo carries the algorithm/schedule separation into accelerator design. Most of the remaining citations are lighter, naming GraphIt among the systems a paper lists or differentiates itself from. The compiler lives on in GraphIt-DSL/graphit, and an evaluated artifact accompanies the paper.
bruening:vee:2012: Reception follows the tool rather than the analysis: the most substantive citations come from systems built on DynamoRIO — fuzzers such as ICS3Fuzzer and Terminator, the Taint Rabbit's taint tracking, and reverse-engineering tools including RePEconstruct, dynStruct, and DYBS — which cite the paper as the account of the platform they run on, often in security settings where transparency against uncooperative code matters. A second group cites its transparency requirements as evidence when discussing what dynamic binary instrumentation can and cannot hide, and Engineering Record and Replay for Deployability takes the system as a point of comparison for its own design. Much of the rest is list membership among instrumentation frameworks.
thies:dna:2006: Reception came chiefly from the design-automation community for microfluidic biochips. There the paper's mixing algorithm, rather than its layered architecture, is the working object: a line of sample-preparation papers — on layout-aware, efficient, robust, and multi-target mixture preparation and dilution — takes it as the baseline method to improve upon, while others build dilution algorithms on its ideas or use it inside larger flows such as assay locking against bio-IP theft. The abstraction-layer argument itself surfaces mainly in passing mentions and survey citations, so in the citing literature the paper functions less as a programming-systems proposal than as the reference dilution algorithm.
urbanski:loc:2006: Beyond that line, the chip found users of its own: the device and its multiphase approach supported fluorescent molecular-logic-gate experiments, and Urbanski and colleagues carried it into metabolic profiling of single preimplantation embryos, while design-automation work on continuous-flow biochips later reused the architecture as a benchmark. Most of the citation record, though, sits in the field's broader literature — Micro Total Analysis Systems reviews and articles on microfluidic large-scale integration cite the paper as one entry in the catalogue of droplet-control techniques. The reception is that of a hardware paper absorbed into its field: a handful of direct uses, and a long tail of passing mention.
hall:sc:1995: Reception in the citing literature runs unusually deep for its size: a large share of the citations come from work that ran the compiler rather than merely naming it. SUIF Explorer built its interactive parallelization support on the system; compiler-directed page coloring drew its parallelized applications from it; and a line of work on software distributed shared memory by Han, Tseng, and Keleher used its output to study runtime support for compiler-parallelized codes. Later work extended the analysis toward coarse-grain pipelining on FPGAs, and predicated array data-flow analysis measured itself against the paper's results. The rest of the record largely cites the coverage figures as evidence of what interprocedural analysis can find.
stephenson:cgo:2005: In the wider literature the paper functions mostly as an early exhibit of machine learning applied inside a compiler: the bulk of its citations are brief mentions in surveys and related-work discussions of learned compilation, citing it as an early demonstration rather than engaging its classifiers. A smaller group adopts the method as a template, training supervised models to predict other decisions — heterogeneous task partitioning, thread-coarsening on graphics processors, transactional-memory tuning, loop iteration counts, and unroll factors in high-level synthesis — while work on automatic feature generation and on selecting optimizations from performance counters measures itself against it. Direct extensions are rare; the paper's reach is as a precedent and a recipe.
babb:fccm:1999: The citing literature received the work mostly as a marker. Its main afterlife is in surveys of reconfigurable computing — Compton and Hauck, Todman and colleagues, Tessier and Burleson — where the compiler stands as an example of carrying sequential C and Fortran all the way to hardware. Engaged citations are few: the DIVA processing-in-memory work differentiates its architecture against this approach, and Rugina and Rinard's pointer analysis for structured parallel programs made use of the compiler. Most other citations name the paper in passing while mapping the space of C-to-gates compilation, so the reception is modest in depth if not in venue.
barua:isca:1999: External reception is modest and stays close to the architecture. In the tiled-processor and reconfigurable-computing literature Maps appears as the worked example of a memory system managed entirely by the compiler — Hartenstein's retrospective on reconfigurable computing lists it in that role, and work on coarse-grain pipelining across FPGA architectures borrows the idea of compiler-orchestrated data placement. The deeper engagements are few: Taylor's account of tiled microprocessors builds on the system, Rugina and Rinard's pointer analysis for structured parallel programs uses it, and modulo unrolling reappears in affine loop optimization for Chapel. Most other citations are brief, and the paper's imprint is best read through the Raw project it served rather than through independent adoption.
bernstein-kjolstad:2016: As a position piece it is cited for its argument, though most of its citation record is unjudged and the judged portion is a handful. That handful comes from the community the argument addressed: the Taichi line of simulation languages invokes it when motivating compiler support for simulation — QuanTaichi and MeshTaichi both cite it — and IMESH, a DSL for mesh processing in the same journal, takes up the argument directly. A study of generating sounds for soft bodies and a SIGGRAPH Talks piece on the look and lighting of Frozen 2 show it reaching practitioners. The article is cited to justify building new simulation languages — the outcome it argued for.
amarasinghe:lcpc:1993: Citations to the overview read it as the citable description of the SUIF parallelizing compiler rather than as a technique paper. Works built on the same infrastructure point to it when describing their setting — linear scan register allocation and Rugina and Rinard's symbolic bounds analysis and recursion unrolling among them — and embedded-systems research on application scenarios cites the compiler as machinery. Elsewhere the paper appears in lists of parallelizing compilers alongside the polytope-model literature. Engagement with the three-phase design itself is rare, and much of the citing record is brief, so the reception is best described as acknowledgment of the infrastructure the overview documents.
thies:nc:2007: External reception centers less on the abstraction layers than on the mixing algorithm beneath them. The digital-microfluidics literature on sample preparation treats the paper's dilution and mixing scheme as a point of departure: work on waste-aware dilution, reactant minimization with skewed mixing trees, and multi-target sample preparation measures new algorithms against it, while error-correcting and error-oblivious sample preparation on digital microfluidic biochips builds on it directly. Beyond that community the record consists mostly of brief mentions in the programmable-microfluidics literature; the layered-abstraction argument itself drew fewer direct successors than the algorithm it carried.
thies:ictd:2009: In the wider literature the paper functions chiefly as evidence: mobile-health and ICTD studies cite its error rates when weighing forms, SMS, and voice against one another, and surveys — from the Cochrane review of self-administered survey questionnaire responses to the account of user interface design for low-literate and novice users — fold it into their pictures of data collection in resource-poor settings. Closer engagement is rarer: Lerer's IVR rendering platform takes the study as its baseline, but few citing papers extend the method itself. Most citations are peripheral, which suits a measured comparison: many papers need the finding, few need more.
sermulins:lctes:2005: Reception concentrates in the stream-programming community the work grew from. The catalog of stream processing optimizations in ACM Computing Surveys records the transformations with this paper among its sources, and detailed discussions outnumber extensions: Moonen's work on predictable embedded multiprocessor architectures carried the cache-aware view to streaming applications on multiprocessor systems-on-chip, later work on generalized cache tiling for dataflow programs measures against the fusion strategy, and stream-processing optimizations for mobile sensing use it as a point of comparison. Others reuse the StreamIt benchmarks the evaluation established, software-pipelined execution of stream programs on GPUs among them. The record is modest in size but grounded: most citations come from people working on the same problem. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure lives on at bthies/streamit.
maydan:popl:1993: Among external citers the paper serves mostly as a reference point: array data-flow and privatization work positions itself against its precision-versus-cost tradeoff, and empirical papers cite its results as evidence that element-wise analysis pays off in parallelization. Direct construction on it is rarer but concrete — SUIF Explorer incorporates the analysis, later work improves and reimplements the accurate array data-flow analysis, and communication-optimization work for parallelizing compilers adopts its exposed-set machinery to eliminate redundant messages. Much of the remaining record is passing mention in surveys of compiler transformations, and a sizable fraction of the external citations is unjudged.
bruening:cgo:2011: In the citing literature Dr. Memory serves chiefly as a yardstick. Memory-error detectors that followed — AddressSanitizer and MemorySanitizer among them — measure their speed and coverage against it, and the pattern repeats across use-after-free detection, uninitialized-read mitigation, firmware fuzzing, and shadow-memory monitoring. A second, larger body of citations places the tool in the standard roster of memory checkers, while binary-only fuzzing work puts the tool itself to use. Few papers build on its internals; its role in the literature is that of an established baseline against which new detectors are measured. The implementation lives on in the DynamoRIO/drmemory repository.
chou:2018:formats: Outside the project, the level-format abstraction became a shared vocabulary for sparse compilation. Works that adopt the idea carry it beyond taco's setting: the Sparse Abstract Machine builds a hardware abstraction around per-dimension level formats, Stardust and SpDISTAL take the approach to reconfigurable dataflow and distributed machines, and compiler work on modular sparse workspaces and sparse tensor convolutions reasons in the same terms. Others use taco itself, from GPU code generation in Sgap to query optimization in Galley. Around this core, a larger body of sparse-systems papers cites the work, often in passing, as one of the compilers that made formats a first-class concern. The implementation lives on in the tensor-compiler/taco repository, and an evaluated artifact accompanies the paper.
thies:ecoop:2005: The citing literature treats the paper mainly as a reference point: most citations are passing mentions in the related work of race and deadlock detectors, and surveys of testing for concurrent software list it among the static approaches. The engaged minority comes from successors in static deadlock detection — Naik, Park, and Sen position their detector against the lock-order-graph analysis — and one study reused its library subjects to compare the cost-effectiveness of static analysis and model checking for finding deadlocks. Few works build on the analysis itself; the paper settled into related-work sections as the treatment of deadlock freedom at the library interface.
ding:pldi:2015: Later work cites the paper mainly as an example. Surveys of compiler autotuning using machine learning, overviews of machine learning in compiler optimization, and accounts of autotuning in high-performance computing cite it as an instance of input-adaptive tuning, and most other references are brief. A smaller group takes up the problem itself: a pattern-based algorithmic autotuner for graph processing on GPUs adopts input-aware algorithmic choice, empirical work on input-aware performance models of configurable systems builds on the framing, and White-Box Program Tuning measures against it. The reception registers the paper as the marker for input sensitivity in autotuning rather than as a system others run. The PetaBricks compiler and its algorithmic-choice infrastructure live on at petabricks/petabricks.
ansel:cgo:2011: External reception came mostly from the approximate-computing literature, which absorbed it as an example. Mittal's survey of approximate computing places it among language-level approaches, a Proceedings of the IEEE retrospective does the same, and the Wang and O'Boyle survey of machine learning in compiler optimization lists its evolutionary search. Systems papers such as Paraprox position their own approximation schemes against its compile-time autotuning, and a smaller band reuses its benchmarks, the canary-input work on dynamically steered approximation among them. Nearly all of these citations are peripheral: the paper is a fixture of related-work sections on trading accuracy for performance, and only EMEURO, an accelerator-generation framework, built on the system directly. The PetaBricks compiler and language are preserved in the petabricks/petabricks repository.
taylor:hpca:2003: Reception runs through the networks-on-chip literature, which absorbed the paper as the account of an extreme design point: on-chip networks whose latencies must be counted in single cycles. Citing works most often invoke its latency and occupancy measurements as evidence for how sensitive partitioned architectures are to operand transport, or place it in related-work discussions of on-chip interconnects; a few reuse its benchmarks. Deeper engagement is rarer. The sharing architecture builds on its ideas, a point-to-point inter-cluster network for clustered superscalar processors measures against it, and the account of the Tile Processor's on-chip interconnection architecture treats it in detail.
zhang:bigdata:2017: The citing literature took up the paper in two roles. Its diagnosis, that fast graph frameworks stall on memory for most of their cycles, is cited as motivating evidence across graph-processing research, and its results serve as a measuring stick: the I-GCN accelerator, hardware-assisted propagation blocking, and learning-based data reordering all compare against CSR segmenting. The technique itself traveled as well. VGL adapted segmenting to the NEC SX-Aurora TSUBASA vector architecture, GNNIE to GNN inference, and HyTGraph builds on the partitioning scheme for GPU-accelerated processing, while work on practical parallel hypergraph algorithms reuses the framework directly. The implementation lives on in the GraphIt-DSL/graphit repository.
phothilimthana:asplos:2013: External readers cite the paper mostly as a marker in the CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing literature rather than as a system to build on. The ACM Computing Surveys treatment of CPU-GPU heterogeneous computing techniques includes it, and work on heterogeneous scheduling, data partitioning, and performance portability — the rewrite-rule generator of OpenCL code among them — names it as the autotuning point in the design space, sometimes pausing over the choice-and-poly-algorithm approach in detail. Direct reuse stays within the PetaBricks project itself; beyond it, the paper's role is that of a cited example of what installation-time autotuning across CPUs and GPUs can achieve. The PetaBricks compiler and language live on in the petabricks/petabricks repository.
thies:pact:2010: In the citing literature the study leads a double life, as evidence and as workloads. Its findings — above all that most filters are stateless — are cited to support design decisions in later streaming languages, runtimes, and schedulers, and the characterized suite itself became a source of evaluation workloads across the embedded-systems literature: hard-real-time scheduling of streaming applications, energy-efficient mapping onto MPSoCs, NoC and CGRA design, and machine-learned partitioning of streaming programs all draw benchmarks from it, and the Savina actor benchmark suite draws on it as well. Few works extend the study itself; its role is to be the empirical ground other designs stand on. The StreamIt compiler infrastructure behind the suite lives on at bthies/streamit.
palkar:vldb:2018: The citing literature treats the paper mainly as a reference for what end-to-end optimization across data-science libraries can achieve: papers on query compilation and analytics systems cite Weld, usually briefly, when motivating or classifying their own designs. A smaller band engages the system directly. Willump builds its machine-learning inference optimizer on Weld; Tuplex and later work on declarative sub-operators measure against it as the composable-optimization baseline; PyTond reuses its data-science workloads; and the split-annotations work on optimizing data-intensive computations in existing libraries returns to the same benchmarks. The reception is concentrated in the database-systems community that the paper addressed. The implementation lives on in the weld-project/weld repository.
ansel:pldi:2011: In the citing literature the paper stands as the reference for making sandboxes admit dynamically generated code. Security work on isolation and control-flow integrity cites it when marking that boundary: MiniBox and the control-flow-integrity papers of Niu and Tan note it as the extension of software-based fault isolation to JIT compilers, and the WebAssembly design paper lists it among the developments around Native Client. Engagement beyond positioning is thinner but concrete — the work on bringing Java's native code under control used its mechanisms directly, and Fay adopted its ideas for safe runtime instrumentation. Most other citations are brief mentions in surveys of sandboxing and memory-safety defenses.
